study_design_identified: Mixed-methods process evaluation embedded within a 100-village cluster-randomised controlled trial (combining documentary review, repeated semi-structured interviews with NGO implementers, longitudinal structured observations of latrine construction, 10% random household and VWSC surveys across randomized arms, and within-intervention village-level linear regressions)
why_tool_chosen: The paper is a primary mixed-methods process evaluation that collects, analyses, and integrates both qualitative data (review of TSC/NGO documents and logs plus 6 rounds of semi-structured interviews with NGO staff and village motivators) and quantitative data (direct observations of household latrine construction, a 10% random household awareness survey across 50 cluster-randomised intervention and 50 control villages, a 10% random VWSC survey, and village-level linear regressions). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT is the designated tool for mixed-methods primary studies; the Quantitative randomized block (2.1–2.5) was selected to match the primary 50-vs-50 cluster-randomised arm comparisons (Figure 1, Table 2), while unadjusted confounding in the secondary within-intervention ecological regressions (Table 4) is explicitly captured in item 5.5 and the cross-tool confounding domain.
overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (narrative MMAT judgment; no numeric score computed — strong physical latrine observation and mixed-methods integration, but constrained by unreported qualitative analysis/quotes, unblinded assessment, incomplete fidelity and logbooks, unreported survey non-response, and unadjusted within-arm ecological regressions)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The Methods section clearly specifies four explicit objectives for the process evaluation: documenting context, documenting intervention delivery, assessing target population exposure, and exploring associations between household exposure to community mobilisation activities and latrine construction.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collected across 6 bimonthly field rounds (document review, NGO motivator interviews, census-level household latrine observations in 50 intervention villages, baseline/follow-up coverage checks in all 100 villages, and 10% random household and VWSC surveys) directly address all four objectives.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining documentary review of TSC guidelines, NGO activity logs, meeting notes, and stock/contribution registers with repeated semi-structured interviews of implementing NGO staff and village motivators was appropriate to capture implementation fidelity, adaptations, and contextual barriers.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Although bimonthly field visits over one year and translation/back-translation of guides into Oriya are reported, the paper provides almost no detail on semi-structured interview protocols, audio-recording or field-note procedures, or qualitative interviews with ordinary villagers, and notes that motivator logbooks varied substantially in completeness.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2–3 of 12, Methods; PDF Page 11 of 12, Discussion, paragraphs 3–4

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: The Methods section explains quantitative statistical procedures in Stata 13 but provides no description of how qualitative interview notes and documentary records were organised, coded, or thematically analysed.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3 of 12, Methods, paragraph 2; PDF Pages 4–7 of 12, Results

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative explanations of implementation bottlenecks (e.g., BPL subsidy disputes, road-project sand shortages, mason attrition, flooding, election halts) align with quantitative patterns, but zero verbatim interview excerpts or structured qualitative evidence tables are presented to substantiate interpretations.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4–7 of 12, Results; PDF Pages 9–11 of 12, Discussion

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: While field sources and overarching conclusions cohere logically, the complete omission of qualitative analytic procedures and primary qualitative quotations prevents verification of full methodological coherence from raw qualitative data to interpretation.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2–3 of 12, Methods; PDF Pages 4–11 of 12, Results and Discussion

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative randomized 2.1: Is randomization appropriately performed?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper states that following a baseline survey, 100 villages were randomly allocated into two study arms (50 intervention, 50 control) and cites the published protocol [6], but does not report the random sequence generation or allocation concealment methods within this manuscript. Within villages, 10% survey subsamples were randomly generated in Stata 13.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 2 of 12, Background, paragraph 2; PDF Pages 2–3 of 12, Methods, paragraphs 4–5

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative randomized 2.2: Are the groups comparable at baseline?
domain_ratings.justification: At baseline (October 2010), household toilet access was identical (8%) in intervention and control villages (Figure 1), and surveyed household respondents in the two arms had comparable age (mean 45 vs 41 years) and female representation (61% vs 56%; Table 2).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4 of 12, Results (Latrine construction); PDF Page 6 of 12, Figure 1; PDF Page 8 of 12, Table 2

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative randomized 2.3: Are there complete outcome data?
domain_ratings.justification: Village-wide latrine observations covered n=4,699 households in March 2012 and n=4,585 in March 2013, and 10% surveys included n=807 households and n=170 VWSC members, but exact non-response/refusal rates are omitted, joint-family reporting caused shifting household denominators, and village-level mobilisation records were missing for 2 to 13 of 50 villages.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11 of 12, Results, Figure 1, Tables 2–3, and Discussion

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative randomized 2.4: Are outcome assessors blinded to the intervention provided?
domain_ratings.justification: Enumerators were not blinded: although separate from implementing NGOs, they visited the 50 intervention villages every 6–8 weeks to interview NGO motivators, review VWSC logs, and inspect visible latrines and wall paintings, and conducted unblinded household awareness interviews.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 2 of 12, Methods, paragraphs 3–4; PDF Page 11 of 12, Discussion, paragraphs 3–4

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative randomized 2.5: Did the participants adhere to the assigned intervention?
domain_ratings.justification: Both delivery fidelity and uptake fell substantially short of plan: completed latrine coverage reached 51% (66% including unfinished/damaged) after one year against a 90% target; participatory PRA/mapping reached virtually no households (0–6% recall); subsidies were expanded from BPL-only to all households; 30% of VWSC members did not know their role; and 49% of control households had heard of the TSC.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 of 12, Results and Discussion, Tables 2–3

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Grounded in Linnan and Steckler's process evaluation framework, the authors justify combining qualitative implementation documentation with quantitative coverage and exposure surveys so trial health outcomes are not misattributed to the TSC intervention as planned rather than as actually delivered.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 2 of 12, Background, paragraph 4 and Methods, paragraph 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative findings from NGO staff/motivator interviews and logs are systematically paired with quantitative latrine trajectories and household/VWSC survey results across fidelity, exposure, and contextual barrier analyses.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4–11 of 12, Results and Discussion

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Integration directly explains key empirical patterns, including why household recall of PRA triggering was near zero (motivators skipped mapping or worked with only 2–3 VWSC members) and why BPL and APL latrine coverage differed by only 7% (implementers extended subsidies to all households to resolve conflict).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4–7 and 9–11 of 12, Results and Discussion

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative results and qualitative findings adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly examine discrepancies between NGO-reported activities and household recall (e.g., mapping reported in 37 villages by motivators vs 6% household awareness) as well as household count discrepancies between NGO registers and enumerator censuses caused by strategic joint-family reporting.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4–7 and 10–11 of 12, Results and Discussion

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Per MMAT standards, methodological quality is constrained by weaknesses in both strands: the qualitative strand omits coding/analytic procedures and verbatim quotes, while the quantitative strand lacks blinding, omits survey response rates, suffers missing village-level logs, and relies on unadjusted bivariate ecological regressions (Table 4) for within-arm associations.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 2–3 and 11 of 12, Methods, Table 4, and Discussion

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate concern / Can't tell for survey non-response: household counts observed for latrine coverage shifted slightly from n=4,699 in March 2012 to n=4,585 in March 2013 (partly reflecting inconsistent joint-family boundary reporting), response/refusal rates for the 10% household (n=807) and VWSC (n=170) surveys are not reported, and village motivator turnover plus local political unrest produced missing process data for 2 to 13 of the 50 intervention villages across specific mobilisation components.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Low-to-moderate concern for the cluster-randomised 50-vs-50 village comparisons of latrine coverage and household awareness (supported by identical 8% baseline toilet access and similar respondent demographics, though randomization mechanics are deferred to the protocol paper [6]); high concern for the secondary within-intervention village-level linear regressions (Table 4, n=50 villages), which are bivariate unadjusted ecological regressions that do not control for implementing NGO, village poverty/caste composition, severe flooding in 13 villages, political unrest, or local sand-price shocks.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Strong-to-adequate programmatic operationalization: the paper accurately details the formal rules of India's Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) / Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA)—including BPL vs APL subsidy eligibility, the June 2011 subsidy increase from INR 2,200 to INR 3,200, VWSC composition mandates, Nirmal Gram Puraskar incentives, and election code-of-conduct halts—and directly tracks de facto street-level deviations from formal guidelines (such as extending subsidies to all households to defuse community conflict and omitting participatory triggering).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern for latrine infrastructure status (assessed independently by trained enumerators via direct household inspection every 6–8 weeks using objective structural criteria, though complicated by strategic household over/under-reporting of joint-family counts); moderate-to-high concern for mobilisation fidelity and awareness measures due to unblinded enumerators, reliance on NGO motivator self-reports and incomplete logbooks, retrospective household/VWSC recall, and absence of direct measurement of actual latrine use.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for latrine construction coverage and programme awareness, but weak/absent for latrine use: physical latrine completion was rigorously observed using explicit structural criteria (walls >1.5 m, door, unbroken/unblocked pan, functional pan-pipe-pit connection) and awareness was captured via translated and back-translated questionnaires, whereas actual latrine use/open defecation behaviour was not measured despite appearing in the study title.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: the parent cluster-randomised trial was prospectively registered (NCT01214785) with a published protocol [6], and implementation shortfalls and null associations are candidly reported, but no pre-specified analysis plan is cited for the process evaluation's 13 exploratory ecological regressions (Table 4) and qualitative findings are summarized narratively without systematic coding tables or verbatim quotations.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern: 100 villages in Puri district were selected with government cooperation and randomly allocated 50:50 to intervention and control arms (sequence generation described in [6]), and 10% household (n=807) and VWSC (n=170) subsamples were randomly selected from village lists in Stata 13; however, sample sizes were logistically determined, survey non-response rates are unreported, absent household heads were replaced by any adult/member >16 years present at the visit, and process documentation missed 2 to 13 intervention villages on several mobilisation items.

overall_narrative_summary: Boisson et al. (2014) report a mixed-methods process evaluation embedded within a 100-village cluster-randomised controlled trial (50 intervention, 50 control villages) of India's Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) in Puri district, Orissa. Appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018; no numeric composite score computed), the study demonstrates strong mixed-methods rationale and integration (5.1–5.4 = Yes), objective longitudinal physical inspection of household latrine construction across six field rounds, random Stata-generated 10% sampling of village household and VWSC lists, and cluster-level statistical comparisons respecting village randomization. However, overall methodological quality cannot exceed its weakest components and warrants moderate-to-high concern: (1) the qualitative component reports no coding or thematic analysis methods and zero verbatim quotations (1.2–1.5 = Can't tell); (2) enumerators could not be blinded (2.4 = No) and relied partly on incomplete NGO motivator logbooks with missing data across 2–13 villages; (3) survey non-response rates are unreported and joint-family boundaries were strategically misreported by households (2.3 = Can't tell); (4) intervention fidelity and uptake fell far short of the 90% target (51% completed latrines, 66% including unfinished/damaged; 2.5 = No), while actual latrine use was not measured; and (5) within-intervention associations between mobilisation awareness and coverage (Table 4) rely on unadjusted bivariate village-level linear regressions vulnerable to ecological confounding.
where_found_summary: Study design and data collection: Abstract (PDF p. 1) and Methods (PDF pp. 2–3). Institutional/legal TSC rules and implementation fidelity: Results—Context, Intervention, and Fidelity assessment (PDF pp. 3–7, Table 1, Figures 1–2). Quantitative awareness surveys and ecological regressions: Results—Exposure to intervention (PDF pp. 7–11, Tables 2–4). Methodological limitations, denominator misreporting, and missing motivator logs: Discussion (PDF pp. 9–11).
